topics.name: Hemoglobin
topics.kicker: Iron-rich protein in red blood cells · Carries oxygen around the body
topics.dates: Structure solved by Max Perutz (Nobel Prize, 1962)
topics.briefing: Hemoglobin is the protein that makes your blood red, and each red blood cell carries hundreds of millions of these molecules. Every hemoglobin molecule has four iron-holding heme groups, so it can grab four oxygen molecules in your lungs and drop them off in your muscles and brain. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it sticks to hemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen does.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Max Perutz shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using X-ray crystallography to work out the shape of this protein, while John Kendrew solved its smaller, single-chain cousin, myoglobin. In most adults, this protein has four chains, two alpha and two beta.
tossups.r: Its four heme groups each hold an iron ion. For 10 points, name this protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

tossups.p: In 1904, Christian Bohr, the father of physicist Niels Bohr, found that carbon dioxide makes this protein let go of oxygen more easily. Acid has the same effect, so this protein unloads extra oxygen in hard-working muscles.
tossups.r: Each molecule of this protein holds four iron-containing heme groups. For 10 points, name this protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

tossups.p: Linus Pauling called sickle-cell disease the first “molecular disease” after finding that it changes this protein, and Vernon Ingram later showed that the change swaps just one amino acid, glutamic acid, for valine in its beta chains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this iron-rich protein that red blood cells use to carry oxygen.

tossups.p: Before birth, a person makes a version of this protein with gamma chains in place of beta chains. That version grabs oxygen more tightly than the adult version, so oxygen can pass from the mother’s blood across the placenta.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells and gives blood its red color.

tossups.p: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds this protein more than 200 times as tightly as oxygen does, crowding the oxygen out. If the iron at this protein’s core loses an electron, changing from the +2 to the +3 state, the protein can no longer carry oxygen.
tossups.r: It normally carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. For 10 points, name this iron-containing protein in red blood cells.

tossups.p: Root nodules of beans and peas turn pink because they hold a plant relative of this protein, which keeps oxygen away from the bacterial enzyme nitrogenase. Antarctic icefish are unusual among vertebrates because their blood has none of this protein at all.
tossups.r: In humans, it is packed inside red blood cells. For 10 points, name this oxygen-carrying protein that makes blood red.

tossups.p: A graph of this protein’s oxygen loading is S-shaped, because once one oxygen molecule binds, the others bind more easily, a pattern called cooperative binding. This protein switches between a tense T state and a relaxed R state as oxygen attaches.
tossups.r: Each of its four heme groups can carry one oxygen molecule. For 10 points, name this protein found in red blood cells.

tossups.p: When worn-out red blood cells are broken down in the spleen, the iron from this protein is recycled, and the rest of its heme becomes green biliverdin and then yellow bilirubin, the pigments that change a bruise’s color as it heals.
tossups.r: Each red blood cell holds hundreds of millions of copies of it. For 10 points, name this iron-containing protein that carries oxygen in the blood.

tossups.p: Octopuses and horseshoe crabs carry oxygen with a copper-based protein that turns their blood blue, but humans use this iron-based protein instead. In humans, this protein turns bright red when it is loaded with oxygen and darker red after it lets go.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein packed inside red blood cells, which carries oxygen from the lungs.

tossups.p: Doctors track diabetes with the A1c test, which measures how much sugar has stuck to this protein over the past few months. Iron-deficiency anemia lowers the amount of this protein in the blood.
tossups.r: Its four heme groups hold iron. For 10 points, name this protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

tossups.p: At high altitude, red blood cells make more of a molecule called 2,3-BPG, which binds this protein and helps it release oxygen to tissues. When oxygen runs low, the kidneys release EPO, telling the bone marrow to make more red blood cells full of this protein.
tossups.r: Low levels of it cause anemia. For 10 points, name this iron-containing protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

tossups.p: The Haldane effect describes how this protein carries more carbon dioxide after it gives up its oxygen. Some carbon dioxide rides on this protein by attaching to amino groups on its chains, though most travels in the blood as bicarbonate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body’s tissues.

tossups.p: In each chain of this protein, a histidine holds an iron ion at the center of a flat porphyrin [“POR-fuh-rin”] ring. Each of those iron-containing heme groups can carry one oxygen molecule, so one copy of this protein carries up to four.
tossups.r: Carbon monoxide can block its oxygen-binding sites. For 10 points, name this protein that makes red blood cells red.

tossups.p: People with thalassemia [“thal-uh-SEE-mee-uh”] make too little of the alpha or beta chains of this protein, which can cause anemia. A single change in the beta chains of this protein can make red blood cells bend into a sickle shape.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this iron-containing protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

tossups.p: A pulse oximeter clipped to a fingertip shines red and infrared light through the skin to estimate how much of this protein is carrying oxygen. Blood rich in oxygen-loaded copies of this protein is bright red, while blood heading back to the heart is darker red, not blue.
tossups.r: A single amino-acid change in it causes sickle-cell disease. For 10 points, name this protein in red blood cells that contains iron.

clues.t: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body
Contains iron, which is where the oxygen binds
Gives blood its red color: bright red when loaded with oxygen, darker red without it (never blue)
Each molecule has four heme groups, so it can carry up to four oxygen molecules
Made of four chains (two alpha and two beta in most adults), a classic example of quaternary structure
Sickle-cell disease comes from a single changed amino acid in its beta chains
Carbon monoxide binds it more than 200 times as tightly as oxygen, crowding the oxygen out
Its single-chain cousin that stores oxygen in muscles is myoglobin
Cooperative binding: each oxygen that binds makes the next bind more easily, giving an S-shaped curve
The Bohr effect: carbon dioxide and acid make it release oxygen more easily in working muscles
The fetal version uses gamma chains and grabs oxygen more tightly than the adult version
Low levels of it, often from too little iron, cause anemia
The A1c test for diabetes measures how much sugar has stuck to it over the past few months
Octopuses and horseshoe crabs use copper-based hemocyanin instead, which makes their blood blue
Max Perutz solved its shape with X-ray crystallography and shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Kendrew (myoglobin)
Christian Bohr, the father of physicist Niels Bohr, described the Bohr effect in 1904
Linus Pauling called sickle-cell disease the first “molecular disease”; Vernon Ingram found valine replacing glutamic acid
2,3-BPG binds it to help release oxygen and rises at high altitude; kidneys release EPO to make more red cells
Haldane effect: it carries more carbon dioxide after giving up oxygen, on amino groups of its chains (most CO2 travels as bicarbonate)
Switches between a tense T state and a relaxed R state as oxygen binds
A histidine holds each iron ion at the center of a flat porphyrin ring
If its iron is oxidized from the +2 to the +3 state, it can no longer carry oxygen
A plant relative turns legume root nodules pink and keeps oxygen away from the enzyme nitrogenase
Antarctic icefish have none of it in their blood
Broken down in the spleen into green biliverdin and yellow bilirubin, the colors of a healing bruise; its iron is recycled
People with thalassemia make too little of its alpha or beta chains
A fingertip pulse oximeter uses red and infrared light to estimate how much of it carries oxygen

trap.title: Hemoglobin, heme, or myoglobin?
trap.body: Heme is only the iron-holding ring inside this protein, and myoglobin is its one-chain cousin that stores oxygen in muscles. They show up together in the same clues: Max Perutz and John Kendrew shared a Nobel Prize, but Perutz solved hemoglobin while Kendrew solved myoglobin. Players also blurt “red blood cells” or “iron” as soon as they hear “carries oxygen.”
trap.fix: “This protein” with four chains, cooperative binding, the Bohr effect, or sickle-cell disease means hemoglobin. “Stores oxygen in muscle” or “a single chain” means myoglobin; “these cells” means red blood cells; “this element” means iron.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hemoglobin (accept haemoglobin, Hb, or Hgb; do not accept “myoglobin” or “heme”)

topics.name: Insulin
topics.kicker: Blood-sugar-lowering hormone · Made by the pancreas’s beta cells
topics.briefing: After you eat, sugar from your food pours into your blood, and your pancreas answers by releasing insulin. This hormone works like a key, signaling muscle, fat, and liver cells to take glucose out of the blood and store it. Before Frederick Banting and Charles Best discovered insulin in 1921, there was no good treatment for type 1 diabetes; today, people with it use insulin shots or pumps.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Frederick Sanger won his first Nobel Prize for working out the order of amino acids in this hormone, the first protein ever sequenced. This hormone’s two chains, called A and B, are held together by disulfide bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone made by the pancreas that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin spent more than thirty years solving this hormone’s three-dimensional structure with X-ray crystallography, finishing in 1969. In the pancreas, this hormone is stored in granules as six-unit clusters held together by zinc ions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone that helps cells take in glucose from the blood.

tossups.p: Working in J. J. R. Macleod’s lab at the University of Toronto in 1921, two researchers extracted this hormone and tested it on diabetic dogs, and James Collip then purified it for use in people. In January 1922, a teenage boy named Leonard Thompson became the first person treated with it.
tossups.r: Those researchers were Frederick Banting and Charles Best. For 10 points, name this hormone that lowers blood sugar and is made in the pancreas.

tossups.p: In 1889, Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering found that removing a dog’s pancreas caused diabetes, a clue that the organ makes this hormone. Twenty years earlier, Paul Langerhans had described the clusters of cells that produce it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone, made in the islets of Langerhans, that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: World Diabetes Day falls on November 14, the birthday of a co-discoverer of this hormone who shared the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with J. J. R. Macleod. That discoverer split his prize money with his young assistant.
tossups.r: The discoverer was Frederick Banting, and the assistant was Charles Best. For 10 points, name this hormone used to treat diabetes.

tossups.p: In 1982, a human version of this hormone made by genetically engineered E. coli bacteria became the first medicine made with recombinant DNA to be approved for people. Before then, patients used this hormone taken from the pancreases of cattle and pigs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone that people with type 1 diabetes need to take.

tossups.p: Beta cells first make this hormone as a longer chain, then cut out a piece called C-peptide, so doctors measure C-peptide to learn how much of this hormone a person’s body makes on its own.
tossups.r: This hormone tells the liver to store glucose as glycogen. For 10 points, name this hormone that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: This hormone binds a receptor tyrosine kinase, which signals muscle and fat cells to move GLUT4 transporters to their surface so they can take in glucose. It also tells fat cells to store fat rather than break it down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: Rosalyn Yalow won a Nobel Prize for the radioimmunoassay, a method that let doctors measure tiny amounts of this hormone in a person’s blood. This hormone is made by beta cells, which sit next to alpha cells in the islets of Langerhans.
tossups.r: Its partner hormone, glucagon, raises blood sugar. For 10 points, name this hormone that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: When glucose enters beta cells, rising ATP closes potassium channels and lets calcium rush in, triggering the release of this hormone, and sulfonylurea [“SUL-fuh-nil-yoo-REE-uh”] drugs work by closing those same channels. Its release climbs after a meal as blood sugar rises.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone from the pancreas that helps cells absorb glucose.

tossups.p: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the cells that make this hormone, while in type 2 diabetes, the body’s cells stop responding to it well. Many people with diabetes check their blood sugar before giving themselves doses of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone, made in the pancreas, that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: Because this hormone is a protein, digestive enzymes would break it apart in the stomach and intestines, so it is usually injected or delivered by a pump instead of swallowed as a pill.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone that people with type 1 diabetes need, which lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: This hormone tells the liver to store glucose as glycogen and slows the liver from making new glucose. Its partner hormone, released by alpha cells, does the opposite by raising blood sugar.
tossups.r: That partner hormone is glucagon, and both come from the islets of Langerhans. For 10 points, name this hormone that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: Somatostatin, released by delta cells, slows the release of both this hormone and glucagon. This hormone’s name comes from the Latin word for “island,” because it is made in small clusters of cells scattered through the pancreas.
tossups.r: Those clusters are the islets of Langerhans. For 10 points, name this hormone that lowers blood sugar.

tossups.p: This hormone contains 51 amino acids, with 21 in its A chain and 30 in its B chain. Taking too much of it can make blood sugar drop dangerously low, a condition called hypoglycemia [“hy-poh-gly-SEE-mee-uh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone from the pancreas that many people with diabetes take to lower their blood sugar.

clues.t: The hormone that lowers blood sugar by helping cells take in glucose
Made by the pancreas
Too little of it, or cells that respond poorly to it, causes diabetes; many people with diabetes take it by injection or pump
Discovered by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto in 1921
Its partner hormone, glucagon, does the opposite job and raises blood sugar
Made by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans; nearby alpha cells make glucagon
Tells the liver and muscles to store glucose as glycogen, and tells fat cells to store fat
In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the cells that make it; in type 2 the body’s cells respond poorly to it
A protein, so digestive enzymes would break it apart; that is why it is usually injected rather than swallowed
In 1982, a human version made by genetically engineered E. coli became the first approved recombinant DNA medicine
Before 1982, patients used versions taken from the pancreases of cattle and pigs
Banting and J. J. R. Macleod won the 1923 Nobel Prize; James Collip purified it for use in people
Its name comes from the Latin word for “island,” after the cell clusters that make it
Too much of it can make blood sugar drop dangerously low, a condition called hypoglycemia
Frederick Sanger worked out its amino-acid order, the first protein ever sequenced (Nobel Prize, 1958)
Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin solved its 3D structure by X-ray crystallography in 1969
51 amino acids in two chains, A (21) and B (30), held together by disulfide bonds
Made first as a longer chain; cutting out the C-peptide frees the active hormone
Stored in granules as six-unit clusters (hexamers) held together by zinc
Binds a receptor tyrosine kinase, which makes muscle and fat cells move GLUT4 glucose transporters to their surface
Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering (1889) found that removing a dog’s pancreas caused diabetes
Paul Langerhans described the cell clusters that make it in 1869
A teenage boy named Leonard Thompson was the first person treated with it, in January 1922
World Diabetes Day, November 14, is Frederick Banting’s birthday
Rosalyn Yalow’s radioimmunoassay let doctors measure tiny amounts of it in blood (Nobel Prize, 1977)
Glucose raises ATP in beta cells, closing potassium channels so calcium triggers its release; sulfonylurea drugs close the same channels
Somatostatin from delta cells slows its release

trap.title: Insulin or glucagon?
trap.body: Both hormones come from the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas and both control blood sugar, but they push in opposite directions: insulin (from beta cells) lowers blood sugar, while glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it. Some tossups in this area want the organ (the pancreas) or the disease (diabetes) instead of the hormone.
trap.fix: Lowers blood sugar, beta cells, Banting and Best, Sanger, or storing glycogen means insulin. Raises blood sugar, alpha cells, or breaking down glycogen means glucagon. “This organ” means pancreas; “this disease” means diabetes.

topics.name: Pancreas
topics.kicker: Gland tucked behind the stomach · Makes digestive enzymes and insulin
topics.dates: About 6 inches (15 cm) long in adults
topics.briefing: The pancreas is a soft, six-inch gland tucked behind your stomach that does two jobs at once. Most of it makes powerful digestive juices that pour into the small intestine to break down proteins, fats, and starches. Scattered through it are tiny “islands” of cells, the islets of Langerhans, that release insulin and glucagon to keep your blood sugar steady.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: George Palade won a Nobel Prize for tracing how proteins travel from the rough ER through the Golgi apparatus and into secretory granules, using the enzyme-making acinar [“ASS-ih-nar”] cells of this organ. Those cells store inactive enzymes in zymogen [“ZY-moh-jen”] granules.
tossups.r: This organ also makes insulin. For 10 points, name this gland that lies behind the stomach.

tossups.p: In 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling discovered secretin, the first hormone ever found, which tells this organ to release bicarbonate. Another hormone, cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], tells this organ to release its digestive enzymes.
tossups.r: Its main duct empties into the duodenum. For 10 points, name this organ that also makes the hormones insulin and glucagon.

tossups.p: This organ ships the protein-cutting enzyme trypsin in an inactive form called trypsinogen, which switches on only when the enzyme enteropeptidase [“en-ter-oh-PEP-tih-days”] meets it in the small intestine. Trypsin then activates this organ’s other enzymes, such as chymotrypsin.
tossups.r: It also releases bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid. For 10 points, name this organ whose islets of Langerhans make insulin.

tossups.p: This organ’s main duct joins the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater [“FAH-ter”], where a ring of muscle called the sphincter of Oddi [“ODD-ee”] controls the flow into the duodenum. A smaller extra duct named for Santorini [“san-toh-REE-nee”] drains part of this organ, too.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that sends digestive enzymes to the small intestine and makes insulin.

tossups.p: A hook-shaped part of this organ called the uncinate [“UN-sih-nate”] process curls behind major blood vessels, while its head sits in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum and its tail reaches toward the spleen.
tossups.r: This organ lies behind the stomach, against the back wall of the abdomen. For 10 points, name this organ that makes insulin.

tossups.p: Cooks call this organ from calves or lambs, along with the thymus, a “sweetbread.” Its name comes from Greek words meaning “all flesh,” and in an adult it is about six inches long.
tossups.r: Its islets of Langerhans make insulin and glucagon. For 10 points, name this gland located behind the stomach.

tossups.p: Surgeons remove the head of this organ, along with part of the small intestine, in the Whipple procedure. Doctors check blood levels of the enzymes amylase and lipase to see whether this organ is inflamed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that makes both digestive enzymes and the hormone insulin.

tossups.p: Ivan Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for studying digestion in dogs, including how nerves control the juice that this organ releases. That juice is rich in bicarbonate, which neutralizes stomach acid as food enters the small intestine.
tossups.r: Its beta cells make insulin. For 10 points, name this organ, home of the islets of Langerhans.

tossups.p: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus can block the ducts of this organ, so many people with the condition take capsules of its enzymes with meals. This organ’s enzymes include lipase, which breaks down fats, and amylase, which breaks down starch.
tossups.r: Its islets of Langerhans release insulin. For 10 points, name this gland that lies behind the stomach.

tossups.p: Only about one or two percent of this organ’s mass is made up of hormone-making islets, which contain alpha, beta, delta, and PP cells. The rest of this organ, made mostly of acinar cells, produces digestive enzymes.
tossups.r: Its beta cells make insulin. For 10 points, name this organ located behind the stomach.

tossups.p: In 1889, Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering showed that dogs without this organ developed diabetes, a sign that it helps control blood sugar. Its alpha cells release glucagon, which raises blood sugar.
tossups.r: Its beta cells release insulin, which lowers blood sugar. For 10 points, name this organ located behind the stomach.

tossups.p: In 1869, a medical student named Paul Langerhans described small clusters of cells scattered through this organ, which were later named for him. In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best extracted a hormone made in those clusters.
tossups.r: That hormone is insulin. For 10 points, name this organ whose islets of Langerhans control blood sugar.

tossups.p: This organ’s duct cells release a fluid rich in bicarbonate that neutralizes acidic chyme [“KYME”] arriving from the stomach. Its acinar cells make amylase for starch, lipase for fats, and protein-digesting enzymes such as trypsin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gland that belongs to both the digestive system and the endocrine system.

tossups.p: If this organ’s trypsin switches on too early, the organ’s own enzymes can start to digest it, causing a painful inflammation. Gallstones that block its duct are a common cause of that inflammation.
tossups.r: Its islets make insulin and glucagon. For 10 points, name this organ, which sits behind the stomach and sends enzymes into the duodenum.

tossups.p: Delta cells in this organ make somatostatin, which slows the release of its other hormones. This organ is both an exocrine gland, sending enzymes through a duct into the small intestine, and an endocrine gland, releasing hormones into the blood.
tossups.r: Its alpha and beta cells make glucagon and insulin. For 10 points, name this organ located behind the stomach.

clues.t: Makes the hormones insulin and glucagon, which control blood sugar
A soft, six-inch gland that lies behind the stomach
Sends digestive enzymes into the small intestine
Its islets of Langerhans hold the hormone-making cells
In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys its insulin-making beta cells
Both an exocrine gland (enzymes through a duct) and an endocrine gland (hormones into the blood)
Its enzymes include amylase (starch), lipase (fats), and trypsin (proteins)
Releases bicarbonate to neutralize acidic chyme arriving from the stomach
Its head sits in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum, and its tail reaches toward the spleen
Islet cells: alpha (glucagon), beta (insulin), delta (somatostatin); the islets are only 1–2% of its mass
The hormones secretin and cholecystokinin (CCK) tell it to release bicarbonate and enzymes
In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus can block its ducts, so many people take its enzymes as capsules with meals
Its own enzymes can digest it if they switch on too early, causing painful inflammation; doctors test blood amylase and lipase
Its main duct joins the common bile duct before emptying into the duodenum
George Palade used its acinar cells to trace the path of secreted proteins (Nobel Prize, 1974)
Its acinar cells store inactive enzymes in zymogen granules
William Bayliss and Ernest Starling found secretin in 1902, the first hormone ever discovered, which acts on it
Enteropeptidase in the small intestine turns its trypsinogen into trypsin, which then activates chymotrypsin and others
Its duct meets the bile duct at the ampulla of Vater, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi
Its main duct is the duct of Wirsung; a smaller extra duct is named for Santorini
A hook-shaped part called the uncinate process curls behind major blood vessels
Cooks call it (or the thymus) from calves and lambs a “sweetbread”
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “all flesh”
The Whipple procedure removes its head along with part of the small intestine
Ivan Pavlov’s Nobel-winning (1904) digestion studies in dogs included how nerves control its juice
Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering (1889) showed that dogs without it developed diabetes
Paul Langerhans described its islets in 1869, while still a medical student

trap.title: Pancreas, liver, or gallbladder?
trap.body: All three organs send juices into the duodenum through connected ducts, so digestion clues overlap: the liver makes bile, the gallbladder stores and squeezes it out, and the pancreas sends enzymes and bicarbonate. Players who hear “islets of Langerhans” or “insulin” also sometimes answer the hormone or the islets instead of the organ.
trap.fix: Bile means the liver (which makes it) or the gallbladder (which stores it). Trypsin, lipase, amylase, bicarbonate, secretin, or islets mean the pancreas. If the question asks for “this organ” or “this gland,” don’t answer insulin or the islets.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pancreas (do not accept “liver” or “gallbladder”)

topics.name: Small intestine
topics.kicker: Longest part of the digestive tract · Where most nutrients are absorbed
topics.dates: About 20 feet (6 meters) long in adults
topics.briefing: Your small intestine is a narrow, coiled tube about 20 feet long, folded up in your belly below the stomach. Its three sections, the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, finish digesting your food with help from bile and pancreatic juice, then absorb nearly all of its nutrients. Millions of tiny, finger-like villi line its walls, giving it a huge surface for soaking up food.
topics.answerHtml: Small intestine (accept small bowel, duodenum, jejunum, or ileum; prompt on intestine, bowel, or gut; do not accept “large intestine” or “colon”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Paneth [“PAH-net”] cells at the bottoms of the crypts of Lieberkühn [“LEE-ber-koon”] protect this organ by releasing germ-killing proteins, while stem cells nearby replace its inner lining every few days. Goblet cells in that lining release protective mucus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this longest section of the digestive tract, where most nutrients are absorbed.

tossups.p: Lacteals [“LAK-tee-ulz”], tiny lymph vessels inside this organ’s villi, absorb digested fats packaged as chylomicrons [“kye-loh-MY-kronz”], while sugars and amino acids enter its capillaries and travel to the liver through the hepatic portal vein.
tossups.r: It follows the stomach in the digestive tract. For 10 points, name this organ lined with finger-like villi, where most digested food is absorbed.

tossups.p: Brunner’s glands in the first section of this organ release alkaline mucus that protects it from stomach acid, and its S cells release the hormone secretin when acidic chyme arrives. That first section also receives bile and pancreatic juice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that connects the stomach to the large intestine.

tossups.p: The final section of this organ absorbs vitamin B12 with the help of a protein called intrinsic factor, and it recycles bile salts so the liver can reuse them. That section also holds clusters of immune tissue called Peyer’s [“PYE-erz”] patches.
tossups.r: That section empties into the large intestine through a valve. For 10 points, name this longest part of the digestive tract.

tossups.p: Oral rehydration drinks mix sugar and salt because this organ’s lining absorbs glucose and sodium together through a carrier protein called SGLT1. The enzyme lactase, made on its lining, breaks down milk sugar, and people who make too little of it are lactose intolerant.
tossups.r: Its walls are lined with villi. For 10 points, name this organ where most digestion and absorption take place.

tossups.p: In people with celiac disease, the immune system reacts to gluten by damaging this organ’s villi, which can flatten them and make it hard to absorb nutrients. Crohn’s disease often affects the last section of this organ.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ, about 20 feet long in adults, that follows the stomach.

tossups.p: The name of this organ’s first section comes from the Latin word for “twelve,” because that section was said to be about twelve finger-widths long. That short, C-shaped section wraps around the head of the pancreas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that receives chyme from the stomach and absorbs most of the nutrients in food.

tossups.p: Circular folds, finger-like villi, and tiny microvilli that form a “brush border” all multiply the surface area of this organ’s lining. Enzymes on that brush border, such as sucrase and maltase, finish breaking sugars down.
tossups.r: It receives chyme from the stomach. For 10 points, name this organ where most nutrients are absorbed into the blood.

tossups.p: This organ’s first section makes cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], or CCK, a hormone that tells the gallbladder to squeeze out bile when fatty food arrives. Its lining also makes enteropeptidase, which switches on the protein-cutting enzyme trypsin.
tossups.r: Most nutrients are absorbed through its villi. For 10 points, name this organ that lies between the stomach and the large intestine.

tossups.p: Waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis push food along this organ, while back-and-forth squeezes called segmentation mix the food with digestive juices. This organ absorbs most of the water that enters the digestive tract, more than the large intestine does.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this narrow, coiled organ, which is about 20 feet long.

tossups.p: Most of the iron in food is absorbed in this organ’s first section, where ulcers caused by the bacterium H. pylori often form. The pyloric sphincter controls how quickly partly digested food enters this organ.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ, the longest part of the digestive tract, whose lining is covered in villi.

tossups.p: A fan-shaped fold of tissue called the mesentery [“MEZ-en-tair-ee”] holds this organ’s loops in place and carries its blood vessels. Its coiled middle section has especially tall circular folds and absorbs a large share of the body’s nutrients.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ, narrower than the large intestine but about four times as long.

tossups.p: Between meals, the hormone motilin triggers sweeping waves of contraction through this organ that clear out leftover food and bacteria, a pattern called the migrating motor complex. Its villi are covered with absorbing cells called enterocytes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ where most of the nutrients from food are absorbed.

tossups.p: Bile salts break fats in this organ into tiny droplets, then form micelles [“my-SELZ”] that ferry digested fats to its lining. Pancreatic lipase and amylase do most of their work inside this organ.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that lies between the stomach and the large intestine and is lined with villi.

tossups.p: In 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling discovered the first known hormone, secretin, after acid placed inside this organ made the pancreas release its juice even though the nerves to that area had been cut. Hormones made here also tell the gallbladder to release bile.
tossups.r: Its lining is covered in finger-like villi. For 10 points, name this organ that receives chyme from the stomach.

clues.t: Receives partly digested food (chyme) from the stomach and passes what is left to the large intestine
Where most digestion is finished and most nutrients are absorbed into the blood
Lined with millions of finger-like villi that add surface area
The longest part of the digestive tract, about 20 feet (6 meters) long in adults
Called “small” for its narrow width, about an inch, not for its length
Has three sections: a short C-shaped first section, a coiled middle section, and a long final section
Its first section receives bile from the liver and gallbladder and digestive juice from the pancreas
The pyloric sphincter controls how quickly food enters it from the stomach
Microvilli on its cells form a “brush border” whose enzymes, like lactase and sucrase, finish digestion
Lacteals in the villi absorb fats; sugars and amino acids enter capillaries that lead to the liver
Peristalsis pushes food along it; segmentation mixes the food with digestive juices
Absorbs most of the water that enters the gut, more than the large intestine does
In celiac disease, the immune system reacts to gluten and damages its villi
Its first section makes the hormones secretin and CCK, which signal the pancreas and gallbladder
Paneth cells at the base of the crypts of Lieberkühn release germ-killing proteins; goblet cells make mucus
Stem cells in its crypts replace its inner lining every few days
Brunner’s glands in its first section release alkaline mucus that shields it from stomach acid
Its final section absorbs vitamin B12 (with intrinsic factor) and recycles bile salts
Its final section holds immune tissue called Peyer’s patches; Crohn’s disease often affects that section
Its first section’s name comes from Latin for “twelve,” for a length of about twelve finger-widths
Digested fats enter its lacteals packaged as chylomicrons; nutrients in its capillaries reach the liver by the hepatic portal vein
Absorbs glucose together with sodium through SGLT1, which is why oral rehydration drinks mix sugar and salt
Its lining makes enteropeptidase, which switches on the pancreas’s protein-cutting enzyme trypsin
Most dietary iron is absorbed in its first section, where ulcers caused by H. pylori often form
A fan-shaped fold called the mesentery holds its loops in place; its middle section has tall circular folds
Between meals, the hormone motilin triggers cleansing waves called the migrating motor complex
Bile salts break fats into tiny droplets and form micelles that carry digested fats to its lining
Bayliss and Starling (1902) found secretin, the first known hormone, by putting acid inside it

trap.title: Small or large intestine?
trap.body: Both are tubes that come after the stomach and both absorb water, so players mix them up; the large intestine is wider but much shorter and holds most of the gut’s bacteria. Saying just “intestine” or “bowel” earns a prompt, so be ready to add “small.” Some tossups ask for one section, especially the duodenum, the C-shaped first part that receives bile and pancreatic juice; the jejunum is the middle and the ileum is the end.
trap.fix: Villi, chyme from the stomach, bile and pancreatic juice, Peyer’s patches, or vitamin B12 mean the small intestine. The appendix, the cecum, the colon, or squeezing the last water out of waste mean the large intestine. When unsure, say “small intestine,” since not every answer line accepts a single section.
trap.line: Real answer line: Small intestine (accept small bowel, duodenum, jejunum, or ileum; prompt on intestine, bowel, or gut; do not accept “large intestine” or “colon”)

topics.name: Plants
topics.kicker: Green organisms that make their own food · The base of most food chains
topics.dates: On land for more than 400 million years
topics.briefing: Plants are living things that make their own food. Their green chlorophyll captures sunlight, and photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water into sugar while releasing the oxygen we breathe. The kingdom stretches from tiny mosses without true roots to giant sequoias such as General Sherman, the biggest single tree on Earth by volume, and every one of them has stiff cell walls made of cellulose.
topics.answerHtml: Plants (accept plant kingdom, Plantae, land plants, or embryophytes; do not accept “fungi” or “algae”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Joseph Priestley found that a sprig of mint could “restore” the air inside a sealed jar in which a candle had burned out. Jan Ingenhousz [“IN-gun-howss”] later showed that these organisms refresh air in this way only when sunlight shines on their green parts.
tossups.r: Their green color comes from chlorophyll. For 10 points, name these living things, including mosses and ferns, that make their own food by photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a tub of carefully weighed soil for five years, found that the soil had lost almost no weight, and concluded that these organisms build their bodies from water. In fact, the carbon in their bodies comes mainly from carbon dioxide taken in through tiny pores called stomata.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organisms that make their own food in chloroplasts and form a kingdom separate from animals and fungi.

tossups.p: Matthias Schleiden [“SHLY-den”] concluded in 1838 that all of these organisms are made of cells, and Theodor Schwann soon said the same about animals. Long before that, Robert Hooke named “cells” after looking at thin slices of cork, which comes from the bark of one of these organisms.
tossups.r: Their cells have rigid walls made of cellulose. For 10 points, name this kingdom of organisms that includes trees, grasses, and flowers.

tossups.p: Theophrastus [“thee-uh-FRAS-tus”], who took over Aristotle’s school, is often called the “father of botany” for his books about these organisms. Carl Linnaeus later sorted these organisms into groups by counting the stamens and pistils in their flowers.
tossups.r: These organisms are producers, the first link in most food chains. For 10 points, name this kingdom of living things that make their own food from sunlight.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin and his son Francis showed that canary grass seedlings bend toward light only when their tips are uncovered. Frits Went later collected the chemical behind that bending, which was named auxin, in tiny blocks of agar.
tossups.r: That bending toward light, called phototropism, helps these organisms catch sunlight for photosynthesis. For 10 points, name these living things, including oaks, ferns, and mosses.

tossups.p: Hormones called gibberellins [“jib-uh-REL-inz”] were discovered in Japan by studying rice seedlings that grew strangely tall because of a fungus, a disease called “foolish seedling.” Another hormone, abscisic [“ab-SISS-ik”] acid, makes these organisms close their leaf pores during droughts.
tossups.r: The gas ethylene makes their fruit ripen. For 10 points, name these living things that use chlorophyll to make their own food.

tossups.p: Thale cress, a small weed in the mustard family, became the first of these organisms to have its genome sequenced, in 2000. Gregor Mendel worked out the basic laws of heredity by breeding thousands of these organisms, all of them peas, in his monastery’s garden.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kingdom of organisms that use chlorophyll to capture sunlight, including peas, cress, and corn.

tossups.p: _Rafflesia arnoldii_ [“ruh-FLEE-zhuh ar-NOLD-ee-eye”], which has the largest single flower of any of these organisms, has no leaves or stems of its own and steals its food from a vine. In the Namib Desert, _Welwitschia_ [“wel-WITCH-ee-uh”] grows only two leaves during its entire long life.
tossups.r: Most members of this kingdom are green from chlorophyll, which captures sunlight for photosynthesis. For 10 points, name this kingdom of living things that includes trees and flowers.

tossups.p: The cells of these organisms trade materials through tiny channels in their walls called plasmodesmata [“plaz-moh-dez-MAH-tuh”]. Their mature cells usually hold a large central vacuole whose water pressure, called turgor pressure, keeps leaves and stems firm.
tossups.r: Their cell walls are made of cellulose. For 10 points, name these organisms whose cells contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: The closest living relatives of these organisms are freshwater green algae called charophytes [“KAIR-uh-fites”], and these organisms began spreading onto land more than 400 million years ago. The earliest of these organisms on land lacked xylem and phloem, much like modern mosses and liverworts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kingdom of organisms that make food by photosynthesis and include mosses, ferns, and flowering species.

tossups.p: The life cycle of these organisms switches between a haploid gametophyte [“guh-MEE-tuh-fite”] stage and a diploid sporophyte [“SPOR-uh-fite”] stage, a pattern called alternation of generations. In mosses the gametophyte is the larger, longer-lived stage, while in ferns the sporophyte is.
tossups.r: Ferns release spores from clusters called sori on the undersides of their fronds. For 10 points, name this kingdom of organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis.

tossups.p: In the flowering members of this kingdom, one sperm cell fertilizes an egg while a second sperm helps form a food-storing tissue called endosperm, a process called double fertilization. Conifers and other gymnosperms in this kingdom instead carry “naked” seeds, often on cones.
tossups.r: Many members of this kingdom move water through xylem and sugars through phloem. For 10 points, name this kingdom of organisms that make food through photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Pairs of guard cells swell or shrink to open and close tiny pores called stomata [“STOH-muh-tuh”] on the leaves of these organisms. Water that evaporates from those pores in a process called transpiration helps pull more water up through tubes of xylem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these living things that take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen as they make food by photosynthesis.

tossups.p: One of these organisms, native only to bogs in the Carolinas, snaps its leaves shut when tiny trigger hairs are touched twice, trapping insects inside. Another one, _Mimosa pudica_, folds up its leaflets within seconds of being touched.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organisms, including the Venus flytrap, that make their own food through photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Robert Whittaker’s 1969 system of five kingdoms placed these organisms beside animals, fungi, protists, and monerans. Unlike fungi, these organisms build their cell walls from cellulose rather than chitin [“KYE-tin”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these producers, which use chlorophyll to make their own food, a kingdom that includes mosses, ferns, and trees.

clues.t: Form their own kingdom of life, separate from animals, fungi, and protists
Make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers at the base of most food chains
Green because of chlorophyll, a pigment packed inside chloroplasts
Their cells have stiff cell walls made of cellulose and usually a large central vacuole
Studied in botany; the kingdom includes mosses, ferns, conifers, and flowering species
Vascular kinds move water up through xylem and sugar through phloem
Nonvascular bryophytes, like mosses and liverworts, lack xylem and phloem and stay small
Tiny leaf pores called stomata, opened and closed by guard cells, let carbon dioxide in
Water evaporating from leaves (transpiration) pulls more water up through the xylem
Gymnosperms, like conifers, have “naked” seeds; flowering angiosperms enclose seeds in fruit and use double fertilization
Alternation of generations: a haploid gametophyte stage alternates with a diploid sporophyte stage
Ferns release spores from clusters called sori under their fronds
Hormones: auxin causes bending toward light (phototropism), and the gas ethylene ripens fruit
The Venus flytrap, native to the Carolinas, snaps shut when its trigger hairs are touched twice
Gregor Mendel worked out the laws of heredity by breeding thousands of peas
Joseph Priestley found a sprig of mint could “restore” air where a candle had burned out; Jan Ingenhousz showed this needs sunlight
Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow for five years; the soil barely lost weight, so he credited water
Matthias Schleiden proposed in 1838 that all of them are made of cells, a step toward cell theory
Theophrastus, who took over Aristotle’s school, is called the “father of botany”
Charles and Francis Darwin showed canary grass bends toward light sensed at its tip; Frits Went collected auxin in agar blocks
Gibberellins were discovered through rice’s “foolish seedling” disease, which makes seedlings grow too tall
Abscisic acid closes their stomata during drought
Evolved from green algae; their closest living relatives are freshwater charophytes
Neighboring cells trade materials through tiny channels in their walls called plasmodesmata
Thale cress (_Arabidopsis thaliana_), a mustard-family weed, was the first of them to have its genome sequenced (2000)
_Rafflesia arnoldii_ has the largest single flower and no leaves or stems of its own; it steals food from a vine
_Welwitschia_ of the Namib Desert grows only two leaves in its whole life
Robert Whittaker’s 1969 five-kingdom system; unlike fungi, their cell walls use cellulose, not chitin

trap.title: Fungi are not plants
trap.body: Mushrooms sprout from soil and stay in one place, so players lump fungi in with this kingdom, but fungi cannot make their own food: they absorb it, and their cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose. Seaweeds and other algae are another trap; they photosynthesize, but most textbooks group them with the protists.
trap.fix: Listen for the food clue. Photosynthesis, chlorophyll, cellulose, xylem, or seeds means plants; hyphae, chitin, mushrooms, or decomposing dead matter means fungi. Clues about single-celled or ocean-floating green life usually point to algae.
trap.line: Real answer line: Plants (accept Plantae or land plants; do not accept “fungi” or “algae”)

topics.name: Polio
topics.kicker: Viral disease that can cause paralysis · Nearly wiped out by vaccines
topics.briefing: Polio is a contagious disease caused by a virus, and in a small share of infections it attacks the nerves that control muscles, causing paralysis. In the early 1950s, American parents dreaded summer outbreaks, until Jonas Salk’s vaccine was announced safe and effective in 1955; Albert Sabin’s oral vaccine followed. A worldwide campaign launched in 1988 has pushed wild polio out of almost every country on Earth.
topics.answerHtml: Polio (accept poliomyelitis, poliovirus, or infantile paralysis; prompt on enterovirus; do not accept “smallpox”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Karl Landsteiner, who also discovered the ABO blood groups, and Erwin Popper showed that a virus causes this disease by passing it to monkeys. Decades later, John Enders, Thomas Weller, and Frederick Robbins won a Nobel Prize for growing that virus in tissue culture, which made it possible to mass-produce vaccines.
tossups.r: Most infections with its virus cause no symptoms at all. For 10 points, name this disease, prevented by Jonas Salk’s vaccine, that can cause paralysis.

tossups.p: The “iron lung” built by Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw in 1928 helped many patients with this disease who could not breathe on their own. During epidemics of this disease in the 1950s, some hospitals filled entire wards with those machines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this viral disease, which vaccines developed by Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin helped nearly wipe out.

tossups.p: Australian nurse Sister Elizabeth Kenny treated patients with this disease using hot, moist packs and gentle exercise instead of the stiff splints most doctors used. Franklin Roosevelt founded a treatment center for people with this disease at Warm Springs, Georgia, where he swam in warm spring water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this viral disease that can cause paralysis, prevented by vaccines from Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin.

tossups.p: Comedian Eddie Cantor coined the name “March of Dimes” when he urged Americans to mail dimes to the White House for a foundation that Franklin Roosevelt started in 1938 to fight this disease. Partly because of that campaign, Roosevelt’s face was put on the dime in 1946.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that Roosevelt was diagnosed with in 1921, which can cause paralysis.

tossups.p: Thomas Francis Jr. led a 1954 field trial of a vaccine for this disease that involved more than a million schoolchildren. The results were announced on April 12, 1955, exactly ten years after the death of Franklin Roosevelt, who had been diagnosed with this disease.
tossups.r: That vaccine was created by Jonas Salk at the University of Pittsburgh. For 10 points, name this viral disease that can cause paralysis.

tossups.p: In a 1955 television interview with Edward R. Murrow, the creator of a vaccine against this disease said that it had no patent, asking, “Could you patent the sun?” That vaccine used virus that had been killed with the chemical formaldehyde.
tossups.r: That creator was Jonas Salk. For 10 points, name this disease that once caused summer epidemics of paralysis.

tossups.p: Huge trials in the Soviet Union in 1959 tested a vaccine for this disease made from live but weakened virus, which was often given to children on sugar cubes. Because that vaccine was swallowed instead of injected, it was cheap and easy to give in mass campaigns.
tossups.r: That vaccine was developed by Albert Sabin. For 10 points, name this viral disease, which Jonas Salk also made a vaccine against.

tossups.p: This disease’s full medical name comes from Greek words for “gray” and “marrow,” because its virus attacks the gray matter of the spinal cord. There, the virus can destroy motor neurons, the nerve cells that tell muscles to move.
tossups.r: Most people infected show no symptoms, but some become paralyzed. For 10 points, name this disease prevented by the Salk and Sabin vaccines.

tossups.p: Of the three types of wild virus that cause this disease, type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019. As of 2024, wild type 1 was still spreading in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan.
tossups.r: A worldwide campaign has worked to wipe out this disease since 1988. For 10 points, name this viral disease that Jonas Salk developed a vaccine against.

tossups.p: The last case of this disease caused by wild virus in the Americas came in Peru in 1991, and India recorded its last such case in 2011. Rotary International has made ending this disease its signature cause since the 1980s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin developed vaccines against.

tossups.p: In 2020, Africa was certified free of the wild virus that causes this disease, four years after Nigeria recorded the continent’s last case. Nelson Mandela had helped launch a 1996 campaign to “kick” this disease out of Africa.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this viral disease that can cause paralysis, which is prevented by an oral vaccine or a shot.

tossups.p: The violinist Itzhak Perlman [“IT-zahk PURL-mun”] had this disease as a child. So did track star Wilma Rudolph, who wore a brace on her leg as a young girl but went on to win three gold medals at the 1960 Olympics in Rome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that can cause paralysis, which Jonas Salk’s vaccine was made to prevent.

tossups.p: Painter Frida Kahlo had this disease at age six, which left her right leg thinner than her left. Franklin Roosevelt was diagnosed with this disease at age 39, in 1921, while vacationing at his summer home on Campobello Island.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that can cause paralysis, which vaccines have nearly wiped out.

tossups.p: In the early 1950s, many American parents kept their children away from swimming pools and movie theaters during the summer “season” of this disease, and 1952 brought the worst outbreak of it in U.S. history.
tossups.r: Its very contagious virus enters the body through the mouth and multiplies in the throat and intestines. For 10 points, name this disease prevented by Jonas Salk’s vaccine.

tossups.p: Rarely, the weakened virus in one oral vaccine against this disease can change and spread in places where few people are vaccinated. In 1988, the World Health Organization, Rotary International, UNICEF, and the CDC launched a global effort to eradicate this disease.
tossups.r: Wiping it out would make it only the second human disease eradicated, after smallpox. For 10 points, name this disease that Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin made vaccines for.

clues.t: Jonas Salk, at the University of Pittsburgh, made the first successful vaccine against it, a shot of killed virus
Albert Sabin made an oral vaccine of live, weakened virus, often given on sugar cubes
A contagious viral disease that can cause paralysis, especially in young children
Franklin D. Roosevelt was diagnosed with it in 1921, at age 39
Iron lungs helped patients who could not breathe on their own
Eddie Cantor named FDR’s 1938 fundraising drive against it the “March of Dimes”; FDR went on the dime in 1946
Salk’s vaccine was announced safe and effective on April 12, 1955, ten years after FDR’s death
Thomas Francis Jr. led the 1954 field trial of Salk’s vaccine, with more than a million schoolchildren
Asked by Edward R. Murrow about a patent, Salk replied, “Could you patent the sun?”
Its virus attacks motor neurons in the spinal cord’s gray matter; its full name comes from Greek for “gray marrow”
Caused by an enterovirus that enters through the mouth; most infections cause no symptoms
Summer outbreaks kept 1950s children out of pools; 1952 was the worst year in U.S. history
A global eradication effort began in 1988 (WHO, Rotary, UNICEF, CDC); it would be the second human disease wiped out, after smallpox
Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw built the iron lung in 1928
John Enders, Thomas Weller, and Frederick Robbins grew its virus in tissue culture (Nobel Prize, 1954)
Karl Landsteiner (who also found the ABO blood groups) and Erwin Popper showed that a virus causes it
Australian nurse Sister Elizabeth Kenny used hot packs and exercise instead of splints
FDR founded a treatment center at Warm Springs, Georgia
Salk’s vaccine used virus killed with formaldehyde
Sabin’s oral vaccine was tested on huge numbers of people in the Soviet Union in 1959
Of three wild types, type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019
As of 2024, wild type 1 still spread only in Pakistan and Afghanistan
The last wild case in the Americas came in Peru (1991); India’s last came in 2011
Africa was certified free of its wild virus in 2020, four years after Nigeria’s last case; Nelson Mandela had helped launch a 1996 campaign to “kick” it out
Track star Wilma Rudolph (three golds in 1960) and violinist Itzhak Perlman both had it as children
Painter Frida Kahlo had it at age six, which left her right leg thinner

trap.title: Disease or doctor?
trap.body: Polio tossups and Jonas Salk tossups share many clues: the 1954 field trial, the April 1955 announcement, and “Could you patent the sun?” Players who hear those clues can blurt “Salk” when the question wants the disease, or “polio” when it asks for the scientist. Don’t confuse polio with smallpox either; smallpox is the only human disease already declared eradicated (in 1980).
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this disease” or “this virus” means polio, while “this scientist” or “this man” means Salk or Sabin. Clues about Edward Jenner, cowpox, or eradication in 1980 point to smallpox instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Polio (accept poliomyelitis, poliovirus, or infantile paralysis; do not accept “smallpox”)

topics.name: Predation
topics.kicker: One organism hunts and eats another · Drives population cycles and arms races
topics.dates: Modeled by Lotka and Volterra in the 1920s
topics.briefing: Predation happens whenever one organism kills and eats another, from a cheetah sprinting after a gazelle to a ladybug munching aphids. Predators and prey are locked in an evolutionary race: hunters get faster, sneakier, or better at spotting food, while prey evolve camouflage, poisons, warning colors, and clever mimicry. When predators vanish, prey populations can explode and reshape a whole ecosystem, which is one reason wolves were brought back to Yellowstone in 1995.
topics.answerHtml: Predation (accept predators, predator–prey relationships, or predatory behavior; prompt on hunting or carnivory; do not accept “parasitism” or “competition”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: G. F. Gause watched the single-celled _Didinium_ [“dye-DIN-ee-um”] devour every _Paramecium_ [“pair-uh-MEE-see-um”] in a test tube and then starve, showing how unstable this interaction can be when victims have no place to hide. Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra wrote paired equations to model this interaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction in which one organism kills and eats another, its prey.

tossups.p: C. S. Holling modeled this interaction by having a blindfolded person tap a tabletop to find sandpaper discs, which led to his “disc equation.” Holling’s three types of “functional response” describe how an animal’s eating rate changes as its food becomes more common.
tossups.r: A lion chasing a zebra is an example of this interaction. For 10 points, name this relationship in which one animal kills and eats another.

tossups.p: Since 1958, scientists have tracked wolves and moose on Isle Royale [“ROY-ul”], an island in Lake Superior, in the longest-running study of this interaction. In that study, the two animals’ populations have risen and fallen partly in response to each other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ecological interaction in which wolves hunt, kill, and eat moose.

tossups.p: Fur-trapping records from the Hudson’s Bay Company show Canada lynx and snowshoe hare populations rising and falling in cycles about ten years long, a classic example of this interaction. In those cycles, lynx numbers peak shortly after hare numbers do.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction between a hunter and the animal it kills and eats.

tossups.p: Robert Paine pried _Pisaster_ [“pye-ZAS-ter”] sea stars off rocks on the Washington coast and found that mussels took over, so he called the sea star a “keystone species.” Sea otters protect kelp forests in a similar way through this interaction, by eating sea urchins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction in which one organism, like a sea star or an otter, kills and eats another.

tossups.p: After wolves returned to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, scientists studied whether fear of these animals changed where elk grazed, a possible “trophic cascade.” Orcas are called “apex” examples of these animals, since no other wild animals hunt adult orcas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these animals, such as lions and wolves, that hunt and kill other animals for food.

tossups.p: Thomson’s gazelles leap high on stiff legs, a behavior called stotting, possibly to show a chasing cheetah that they are too fit to catch. Animals that are often hunted tend to have eyes on the sides of their heads, while hunters tend to have forward-facing eyes for judging distance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction in which an animal like a cheetah kills and eats its prey.

tossups.p: Periodical cicadas emerge by the billions every 13 or 17 years, overwhelming birds and other hungry animals with a defense against this interaction called “satiation.” Some scientists think those prime-numbered cycles help the cicadas avoid enemies with shorter life cycles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction, seen when a frog snaps up and eats a fly.

tossups.p: Henry Walter Bates studied Amazon butterflies and described a kind of mimicry in which a harmless species copies the warning colors of a dangerous one, fooling animals that would otherwise eat it. Hoverflies striped like wasps use that defense against this interaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction in which one animal hunts, kills, and eats another, its prey.

tossups.p: In Müllerian [“myoo-LEER-ee-un”] mimicry, two harmful species share the same warning pattern, so the animals that might eat them learn to avoid both. Bright warning colors, like those of poison dart frogs, are called aposematism [“ap-uh-SEE-muh-tiz-um”], another defense against this interaction.
tossups.r: Camouflage is a defense against it, too. For 10 points, name this interaction in which one organism kills and eats another.

tossups.p: Female _Photuris_ [“foh-TOOR-is”] fireflies copy the flash signals of other firefly species to lure in males, which they then eat, an example of “aggressive mimicry” used in this interaction. Deep-sea anglerfish dangle glowing lures in front of their mouths for the same purpose.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction in which one organism, the hunter, catches and eats its prey.

tossups.p: Garter snakes in the Pacific Northwest have evolved resistance to tetrodotoxin [“teh-TROH-duh-tox-in”], the poison in the rough-skinned newts they eat, while the newts have evolved even more toxin, an evolutionary “arms race” driven by this interaction.
tossups.r: An owl catching a mouse is another example. For 10 points, name this interaction in which one animal kills and eats another.

tossups.p: In 1888 and 1889, vedalia [“vuh-DAY-lee-uh”] beetles from Australia were brought to California, where they saved citrus groves by eating cottony cushion scale insects, an early success of biological control based on this interaction. Gardeners release other ladybugs to eat aphids in the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ecological interaction in which one organism kills and eats another, called its prey.

tossups.p: Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s poem _In Memoriam A.H.H._ describes nature as “red in tooth and claw,” a phrase often used for this interaction. In science classes, students learn about this interaction by pulling apart owl pellets to find the tiny bones of animals the owls swallowed.
tossups.r: A hawk catching a mouse is another example. For 10 points, name this relationship between a hunting animal and its prey.

tossups.p: In this interaction, energy moves up a food chain when one consumer eats another, and the animals that do the eating are usually less common than the animals they eat. Many animals avoid this interaction by using camouflage to blend into their surroundings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this interaction, in which a lion might kill and eat a zebra.

clues.t: An interaction in which one organism hunts, kills, and eats another, its prey
Classic examples: lions and zebras, owls and mice, wolves and elk
Moves energy up food chains when one consumer eats another
“Apex” hunters at the top of a food chain, like adult orcas, have no natural enemies
Hunters tend to have forward-facing eyes; hunted animals often have eyes on the sides of the head
Canada lynx and snowshoe hare numbers rise and fall in roughly 10-year cycles (Hudson’s Bay Company records)
Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra wrote paired equations to model it
Prey defenses include camouflage and bright warning colors (aposematism), as on poison dart frogs
Batesian mimicry (from Henry Walter Bates’s study of Amazon butterflies): a harmless species copies a dangerous one, like a wasp-striped hoverfly
Müllerian mimicry: two harmful species share the same warning pattern
Robert Paine removed _Pisaster_ sea stars, mussels took over, and he coined “keystone species”
Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone in 1995, and scientists study their effects on elk
Students pull apart owl pellets, coughed-up bundles of bones and fur, to see what owls ate
G. F. Gause’s _Didinium_ ate every _Paramecium_ in a tube and then starved; when the prey had a hiding place, some of them survived
C. S. Holling’s “disc equation” came from a blindfolded person finding sandpaper discs; he described three types of functional response
Wolves and moose on Isle Royale in Lake Superior have been studied since 1958, the longest such study
Sea otters eat sea urchins, keeping urchins from destroying kelp forests
Effects of a top hunter that ripple down through a food web are called a trophic cascade
Periodical cicadas swamp birds by emerging by the billions every 13 or 17 years, a defense called satiation
Gazelles leap stiff-legged (stotting), possibly to show a cheetah they are too fit to catch
Female _Photuris_ fireflies fake other species’ flashes to lure and eat males (aggressive mimicry)
Deep-sea anglerfish dangle glowing lures in front of their mouths
Garter snakes evolved resistance to the tetrodotoxin of rough-skinned newts, an evolutionary arms race
Vedalia beetles brought from Australia to California in 1888–89 ate scale insects that were ruining citrus (biological control)
Tennyson’s _In Memoriam A.H.H._ calls nature “red in tooth and claw”

trap.title: Predation or parasitism?
trap.body: Both interactions help one organism at another’s expense, so players mix them up. A predator kills and eats its prey, usually all at once, while a parasite, like a tick or a tapeworm, lives on or inside its host and usually does not kill it right away. Herbivory (eating plants) and competition (fighting over the same resources) are separate interactions too.
trap.fix: Ask whether the eater kills its victim and moves on (predation) or stays attached for a long time (parasitism). If both species lose by sharing food or space, it is competition; if both benefit, it is mutualism.
trap.line: Real answer line: Predation (accept predators or predator–prey relationships; do not accept “parasitism”)

topics.name: Proteins
topics.kicker: Folded chains of amino acids · They do most of the work in every cell
topics.briefing: Proteins are long chains of amino acids that fold into precise 3D shapes, and each shape decides the job. Some are enzymes that speed up chemical reactions, some are antibodies that fight germs, and some, like keratin and collagen, build hair, nails, and skin. Cells build them on ribosomes by following instructions copied from genes, so a single change in a gene can change a protein’s shape.
topics.answerHtml: Proteins (accept protein or polypeptides; prompt on peptides; do not accept “amino acids” or “enzymes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Cyrus Levinthal pointed out that one of these molecules could never fold in a reasonable time by randomly testing every possible shape, yet many fold in less than a second. Christian Anfinsen showed that one of these molecules, ribonuclease, refolds correctly on its own after being unfolded, evidence that its sequence determines its shape.
tossups.r: Ribosomes link amino acids together to build these molecules. For 10 points, name these large molecules, such as enzymes and antibodies.

tossups.p: In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared a Nobel Prize for AlphaFold, an artificial intelligence program that predicts the folded shapes of these molecules. David Baker shared the same prize for designing brand-new examples of these molecules on computers.
tossups.r: Ribosomes build these molecules by linking amino acids. For 10 points, name these biomolecules, which include enzymes and antibodies.

tossups.p: Linus Pauling and Robert Corey proposed two common patterns in the shapes of these molecules, the alpha helix and the beta pleated sheet, which are held together by hydrogen bonds. Those patterns make up the secondary level of these molecules’ structure.
tossups.r: Most enzymes are examples of these molecules. For 10 points, name these molecules made of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

tossups.p: Frederick Sanger won his first Nobel Prize for working out the exact order of building blocks in one of these molecules, insulin. That order, which is spelled out by a gene, is called the primary structure of one of these molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these large molecules that ribosomes build from chains of amino acids.

tossups.p: John Kendrew used X-ray crystallography to reveal the first three-dimensional structure of one of these molecules, myoglobin, while Max Perutz solved hemoglobin, which has four subunits. Hemoglobin’s four fitted-together chains are an example of these molecules’ quaternary [“KWAH-ter-nair-ee”] structure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biomolecules made of amino acids, which include enzymes and antibodies.

tossups.p: Jöns Jacob Berzelius [“ber-ZEE-lee-us”] suggested the name for this class of molecules in 1838, from a Greek word meaning “primary” or “of first importance.” Unlike carbohydrates and fats, these molecules always contain nitrogen, in the amino groups of their building blocks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of nutrients, found in meat, eggs, and beans, that are made of amino acids.

tossups.p: Stanley Prusiner won a Nobel Prize for discovering prions [“PREE-onz”], misfolded versions of these molecules that force normal copies to misfold, leading to mad cow disease. Sickle-cell disease comes from changing just one building block in one of these molecules, hemoglobin, where valine replaces glutamic acid.
tossups.r: Ribosomes build these molecules from amino acids. For 10 points, name these large biomolecules, which include enzymes, antibodies, and keratin.

tossups.p: Barrel-shaped “chaperones” such as GroEL give newly made copies of these molecules a sheltered space in which to fold into the right shape. Cells tag worn-out examples of these molecules with a small marker called ubiquitin [“yoo-BIK-wih-tin”] so they can be chopped up and recycled.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules, such as enzymes and antibodies, that are made of chains of amino acids.

tossups.p: Cooking an egg turns its clear white solid and opaque because heat unfolds, or denatures, these molecules in it. Strong acids and bases can also denature these molecules, destroying the shapes that let them do their jobs.
tossups.r: Most enzymes are examples of these molecules. For 10 points, name these biomolecules, which are chains of amino acids.

tossups.p: In the lab, a blue solution called biuret [“bye-yuh-RET”] reagent turns violet when mixed with these molecules, because it reacts with the bonds that link their building blocks. Those bonds, called peptide bonds, form in dehydration synthesis reactions that each release a molecule of water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these nutrients found in meat and beans, which are made of amino acids.

tossups.p: Hair perms work by breaking and remaking disulfide bridges, links between sulfur atoms on cysteine [“SIS-teen”] units that help hold these molecules in shape. Collagen, the most abundant one of these molecules in the human body, is a fibrous example.
tossups.r: Keratin, which makes up hair and nails, is another one. For 10 points, name these large biomolecules built from amino acids.

tossups.p: Each chain in these molecules has an amino end, called the N-terminus, and a carboxyl end, called the C-terminus. Their building blocks come in 20 common kinds, each with a different side chain, or R group.
tossups.r: Ribosomes build these molecules starting from the amino end. For 10 points, name these molecules whose structure has primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary levels.

tossups.p: A glowing green example of these molecules, first found in the jellyfish _Aequorea victoria_ [“ee-KWOR-ee-uh vik-TOR-ee-uh”], earned a 2008 Nobel Prize because it lets scientists make living cells light up. The largest known one of these molecules, titin [“TYE-tin”], works like a spring inside muscle cells.
tossups.r: Actin and myosin, which make muscles contract, are also examples of these molecules. For 10 points, name these large molecules built from amino acids.

tossups.p: Water-fearing side chains tend to cluster in the middle of these molecules as they fold, helping form their tertiary [“TUR-shee-air-ee”] structure. In some of these molecules, several folded chains fit together, forming a quaternary structure.
tossups.r: Ribosomes assemble these molecules by reading messenger RNA. For 10 points, name these macromolecules made of amino acids.

tossups.p: Messenger RNA carries instructions from DNA to ribosomes, where they are translated into these molecules, the last step of the “central dogma” of molecular biology. Antibodies that fight germs and the hormone insulin are both examples of these molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these nutrients found in meat, eggs, and beans, which are made of amino acids.

clues.t: Chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds
Built by ribosomes, which translate messenger RNA, the last step of the “central dogma”
A nutrient in meat, eggs, beans, and nuts that the body uses to build and repair tissue
Most enzymes, all antibodies, and hormones like insulin are examples
Built from 20 common kinds of building blocks, each with a different side chain (R group)
Have up to four levels of structure: primary (the amino acid order), secondary, tertiary, and quaternary
Secondary structure: alpha helices and beta pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds
Quaternary structure: several chains fit together, like hemoglobin’s four subunits
Heat or harsh acids and bases unfold (denature) them, as when an egg white turns solid
Biuret reagent turns from blue to violet when they are present
Each peptide bond forms by dehydration synthesis, releasing a molecule of water
Disulfide bridges between cysteines hold their shape; hair perms break and remake them
Collagen is the most abundant one in the human body; keratin makes up hair and nails
Sickle-cell disease comes from one change in hemoglobin: valine replaces glutamic acid
Levinthal’s paradox: a chain could never test every shape in time, yet many fold in under a second
Christian Anfinsen showed unfolded ribonuclease refolds by itself, so sequence determines shape
AlphaFold predicts their shapes; Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with designer David Baker
Linus Pauling and Robert Corey proposed the alpha helix and beta sheet (1951)
Frederick Sanger first worked out the full amino acid order of one, insulin (his first Nobel Prize, 1958)
John Kendrew (myoglobin) and Max Perutz (hemoglobin) solved the first 3D shapes with X-ray crystallography
Jöns Jacob Berzelius suggested their name in 1838, from a Greek word meaning “primary”
Prions are misfolded ones that make normal copies misfold, causing mad cow disease (Stanley Prusiner, Nobel 1997)
Barrel-shaped chaperones like GroEL give new chains a sheltered space to fold
Cells tag worn-out ones with ubiquitin so they get broken down and recycled
Each chain runs from an amino end (N-terminus) to a carboxyl end (C-terminus); ribosomes build from the amino end
Titin, a spring-like giant in muscle, is the largest known one
A glowing green one from the jellyfish _Aequorea victoria_ earned the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry

trap.title: The chain, not the link
trap.body: Many tossups describe the building blocks on the way to the giveaway (20 kinds, R groups, amino and carboxyl ends), and players buzz with “amino acids,” which are the links, not the chain. Others hear “enzyme,” “hemoglobin,” or “keratin” and name a single example instead of the whole class of molecules.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these monomers” or a unit with one side chain, say amino acids. If it describes folding, levels of structure, or jobs like speeding up reactions and fighting germs, say proteins (polypeptides is also fine).
trap.line: Real answer line: Proteins (accept polypeptides; prompt on peptides; do not accept “amino acids” or “enzymes”)

topics.name: Punnett squares
topics.kicker: Grid that predicts offspring genotypes · Dominant, recessive, and heterozygous
topics.briefing: A Punnett square is a simple grid that predicts what offspring might inherit. Write one parent’s alleles across the top and the other’s down the side, fill in the boxes, and you can see why two heterozygous parents (Aa) have a 1-in-4 chance of a child with the recessive trait. It is named for Reginald Punnett, a British geneticist who helped spread Gregor Mendel’s ideas in the early 1900s.
topics.answerHtml: Punnett square (accept Punnett squares; prompt on Punnett alone; do not accept “heterozygous” or “pedigree”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The namesake of this diagram asked his friend, the mathematician G. H. Hardy, why a dominant trait does not simply grow more common in a population with each generation. Hardy’s 1908 answer, which showed that allele frequencies stay steady unless something disturbs them, became part of the Hardy–Weinberg principle.
tossups.r: This grid lists one parent’s alleles across its top and the other’s down its side. For 10 points, name this chart used to predict offspring genotypes.
