tossups.p: Working with William Bateson, the namesake of this diagram noticed that flower color and pollen shape in sweet peas were inherited together far more often than expected, an early hint of genetic linkage. In this diagram, each small box shows one possible combination of alleles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid used to predict the results of a genetic cross, such as a 3-to-1 ratio of dominant to recessive traits.

tossups.p: Gregor Mendel counted 5,474 round seeds and 1,850 wrinkled ones after letting heterozygous pea hybrids pollinate themselves, a nearly 3-to-1 result that this diagram predicts. A two-by-two version of this diagram shows why about one fourth of such offspring have the recessive trait.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid whose boxes show the possible genotypes of offspring from a genetic cross.

tossups.p: The forked-line method, or branch diagram, is a shortcut that replaces this tool when a cross involves many genes at once, since this tool would need 64 boxes for a cross of three genes. A typical two-gene cross with this tool needs 16 boxes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid that geneticists use to predict the genotypes of offspring from two parents.

tossups.p: When one gene masks another, which is called epistasis [“ih-PISS-tuh-sis”], this tool can show why two black Labrador retrievers carrying hidden alleles may have puppies in a ratio of 9 black to 3 chocolate to 4 yellow. Without epistasis, the same kind of two-gene cross gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid, named for a British geneticist, used to predict the possible offspring of a genetic cross.

tossups.p: Crosses of yellow mice studied by Lucien Cuénot [“kway-NOH”] gave a 2-to-1 ratio instead of the 3-to-1 ratio this diagram usually predicts, because inheriting two copies of the yellow allele is lethal. Tailless Manx cats show the same pattern.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid that predicts ratios like 3-to-1 by listing each parent’s alleles along its edges.

tossups.p: Thomas Hunt Morgan’s discovery of a white-eyed male fruit fly in 1910 led him to show that some traits are carried on the X chromosome. Versions of this tool for such sex-linked traits label each allele on an X or a Y.
tossups.r: One shows that a carrier mother can expect about half of her sons to be color-blind. For 10 points, name this grid used to predict the genotypes of offspring.

tossups.p: The namesake of this tool co-founded the _Journal of Genetics_ with William Bateson in 1910. This tool can explain how Queen Victoria, a carrier of the blood-clotting disorder hemophilia, passed that X-linked allele to some of her children, spreading it into the royal families of Spain and Russia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid that uses capital letters for dominant alleles and lowercase letters for recessive ones.

tossups.p: Carriers of the sickle-cell allele, who are heterozygous, resist malaria better than noncarriers, an example of heterozygote advantage. This tool shows that two such carriers have a 1-in-4 chance with each child of passing on two copies of the allele.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid whose boxes show the possible genotypes of offspring.

tossups.p: Carl Correns studied four o’clock flowers in which crossing red and white parents gives pink offspring, a case of incomplete dominance. For such flowers, this tool predicts that crossing two pink ones yields red, pink, and white offspring in a 1-to-2-to-1 ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid used in genetics to show every possible combination of the parents’ alleles.

tossups.p: This tool shows that a parent with type A blood and a parent with type B blood, if each carries a hidden O allele, can have children with any of the four blood types. Type AB blood shows codominance, as do roan cattle with both red and white hairs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid that predicts the possible genotypes of offspring from a genetic cross.

tossups.p: In a test cross, an individual with a dominant trait is crossed with a homozygous recessive one, and this tool shows that any offspring with the recessive trait prove the first parent was heterozygous. Breeders use that kind of cross to reveal hidden recessive alleles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grid that lists one parent’s alleles across the top and the other’s down the side.

tossups.p: A four-by-four version of this tool, with 16 boxes, predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio for a cross between two plants that are each heterozygous for two genes, as long as the genes assort independently. A two-by-two version has four boxes, each standing for a 25 percent chance.
tossups.r: Its rows and columns hold each parent’s possible gametes. For 10 points, name this grid used to predict the results of genetic crosses.

tossups.p: For a cross of two heterozygotes, this tool predicts a genotype ratio of 1 homozygous dominant to 2 heterozygous to 1 homozygous recessive, which produces a 3-to-1 ratio of phenotypes when one allele is completely dominant.
tossups.r: Capital letters on this tool stand for dominant alleles. For 10 points, name this grid that shows the possible offspring of two parents.

tossups.p: This tool is named for a British geneticist who worked with William Bateson at Cambridge in the early 1900s, soon after scientists rediscovered Gregor Mendel’s work. To use it, write each parent’s possible gametes along two edges and fill every box with the alleles beside it and above it.
tossups.r: Each box shows one possible genotype. For 10 points, name this grid that predicts the genotypes of a cross’s offspring.

clues.t: A grid used to predict the possible genotypes of offspring from a genetic cross
One parent’s alleles go across the top, the other’s down the side; each box is one possible offspring
Crossing two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa) gives a 3-to-1 ratio of dominant to recessive traits
Capital letters stand for dominant alleles; lowercase letters stand for recessive ones
Heterozygous means two different alleles (Aa); homozygous means two of the same (AA or aa)
Named for a British geneticist who worked with William Bateson at Cambridge in the early 1900s
A cross of two heterozygotes gives a 1:2:1 genotype ratio (AA : Aa : aa)
A dihybrid (two-gene) cross uses a 4-by-4 grid of 16 boxes and gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio
In a 2-by-2 grid, each of the four boxes stands for a 25 percent chance
A test cross with a homozygous recessive individual reveals whether a dominant-looking one is AA or Aa
Gregor Mendel’s pea crosses (round vs. wrinkled seeds, tall vs. short stems) are the classic examples
Incomplete dominance (Carl Correns’s four o’clocks): red × white gives pink, and pink × pink gives a 1:2:1 color ratio
Codominance: both alleles show, as in type AB blood and roan cattle
Sex-linked versions label alleles on X and Y chromosomes; each son of a carrier mother has a 1-in-2 chance of being color-blind
Its namesake asked mathematician G. H. Hardy why dominant traits don’t keep growing more common, leading to the Hardy–Weinberg principle (1908)
Its namesake and Bateson found sweet pea flower color and pollen shape inherited together, an early hint of linkage
Its namesake co-founded the _Journal of Genetics_ with William Bateson in 1910
Mendel counted 5,474 round seeds to 1,850 wrinkled ones, close to 3-to-1
The forked-line method (branch diagram) is a shortcut for crosses with many genes
A three-gene cross would need an 8-by-8 grid with 64 boxes
Epistasis in Labrador retrievers gives 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow
Lucien Cuénot’s yellow mice gave a 2-to-1 ratio because two yellow alleles are lethal (true of tailless Manx cats, too)
Thomas Hunt Morgan’s white-eyed male fruit fly (1910) showed some traits ride on the X chromosome
Queen Victoria carried hemophilia and passed it into the royal families of Spain and Russia
Sickle-cell carriers resist malaria (heterozygote advantage); two carriers have a 1-in-4 chance per child of passing on two copies
Type A (with a hidden O) × type B (with a hidden O) can give children of all four blood types

trap.title: The tool, not the vocabulary
trap.body: Tossups about this grid are packed with genetics words (heterozygous, homozygous, dominant, recessive, genotype), and nervous players buzz with one of those. Others answer “Mendel” or “dihybrid cross,” which are the scientist and the kind of cross, not the diagram. A pedigree is a different chart altogether: it tracks a trait through a real family tree.
trap.fix: If the question says “this diagram,” “this grid,” or “this tool,” say “Punnett square.” Save “heterozygous” for a question asking for the term for having two different alleles, and “pedigree” for a family-tree chart of circles and squares.
trap.line: Real answer line: Punnett square (prompt on Punnett; do not accept “heterozygous” or “pedigree”)

topics.name: Roots
topics.kicker: Underground plant organs · Anchor the plant and soak up water and minerals
topics.dates: Grow from the radicle of a sprouting seed
topics.briefing: Roots anchor a plant and drink for it, soaking up water and minerals through countless microscopic root hairs. Some store food, which is why we eat carrots, beets, and sweet potatoes, though an ordinary potato is actually a stem. Others grow in surprising directions: mangroves send “breathing” roots up out of the mud, and banyan trees drop roots from their branches that thicken into pillars.
topics.answerHtml: Roots (accept root, root system, or taproot; prompt on root hairs, root cap, or radicle; do not accept “stems” or “rhizomes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A waxy band of suberin [“SOO-ber-in”] called the Casparian [“kas-PAIR-ee-un”] strip runs through the cell walls of the endodermis in these organs, forcing water and minerals to pass through living cell membranes before reaching the xylem. Just inside that endodermis lies the pericycle, where new side branches of these organs begin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that absorb water and minerals from the soil and anchor plants in the ground.

tossups.p: Starch-filled grains called statoliths settle to the bottom of cells near the tips of these organs, telling them which way is down. That signal lets these organs bend toward gravity, a response called positive gravitropism.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that grow down into the soil to soak up water, protected at their tips by a cap of cells.

tossups.p: A cluster of slowly dividing cells called the quiescent [“kwee-ESS-ent”] center sits near the tip of these organs. Behind each tip, these organs have a zone of cell division, a zone of elongation where cells stretch, and a zone of maturation where tiny hairs sprout.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that absorb water and minerals from the soil and hold plants in place.

tossups.p: Water entering these organs can travel through cell walls, called the apoplast, or through the cytoplasm of cells joined by tiny channels, called the symplast. Pressure built up in these organs at night can push droplets of water out of the leaf edges of grasses and strawberries, a process called guttation [“guh-TAY-shun”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs covered in tiny hairs that absorb water and minerals from the soil.

tossups.p: Orchids that grow high on tree branches have aerial versions of these organs wrapped in a spongy, silvery layer called velamen [“vuh-LAY-men”] that soaks up rainwater. Banyan trees drop aerial ones from their branches that thicken into pillars looking like extra trunks.
tossups.r: Most of these organs grow underground. For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor a plant and absorb water from the soil.

tossups.p: Black mangroves grow pneumatophores [“noo-MAT-uh-forz”], special versions of these organs that poke up out of the mud like snorkels to take in air. Red mangroves and corn plants are braced by “prop” versions of these organs that grow down from their stems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, which usually grow underground to absorb water and minerals.

tossups.p: Most plants trade sugar to fungi that grow around or into these organs, forming partnerships called mycorrhizae [“my-koh-RYE-zee”] that help them collect water and phosphorus. Legumes like peas also house nitrogen-fixing _Rhizobium_ [“rye-ZOH-bee-um”] bacteria in nodules on these organs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor a plant and absorb water from the soil, often through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Black walnut trees release juglone [“JOO-glone”], a chemical that harms nearby tomato plants, partly from these organs, an example of allelopathy [“uh-lee-LOP-uh-thee”]. The tips of these organs make much of a plant’s supply of cytokinins [“sye-toh-KYE-ninz”], hormones that trigger cell division.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that absorb water and minerals, often through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Dodder, a parasitic vine, loses these organs once it latches onto a host and then feeds through suckers called haustoria [“haw-STOR-ee-uh”]. Mosses have no true versions of these organs and instead cling to surfaces with thread-like rhizoids [“RYE-zoydz”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, which in most plants anchor them in the soil and absorb water.

tossups.p: Lilies and many other bulb-forming plants grow contractile versions of these organs, which shrink lengthwise to tug the bulb deeper into the soil. Sweet potatoes and cassava are swollen versions of these organs, but ordinary potatoes are not; potatoes are underground stems called tubers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, including edible carrots and beets, that absorb water from the soil.

tossups.p: The radicle [“RAD-ih-kul”], the first part of a sprouting seed to break out of the seed coat, develops into the first of these organs. As one of these organs pushes through soil, the protective cap at its tip is constantly worn away and replaced.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor a plant and absorb water through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Versions of these organs that grow from a stem or leaf, instead of from the radicle of a seed, are called adventitious [“ad-ven-TISH-us”]. Gardeners dip stem cuttings in powders containing auxins, such as IBA, to make new ones of these organs sprout.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that grow underground and absorb water and minerals from the soil.

tossups.p: In buttercups and other eudicots, the xylem at the center of these organs forms an X or star shape when cut crosswise, while in corn and other monocots the xylem and phloem form a ring around a soft central pith.
tossups.r: Grasses usually have a fibrous system of these organs instead of one thick main one. For 10 points, name these underground plant organs that absorb water and minerals.

tossups.p: Overwatering can kill a houseplant because soggy soil leaves these organs without the oxygen they need for cellular respiration. Most of these organs lack chlorophyll, so they depend on sugar sent down from the leaves through the phloem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that take in water and minerals through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Dandelions are hard to pull up because they have one long, thick main one of these organs, while grasses form a fibrous mat of thin ones that helps hold soil in place and prevent erosion.
tossups.r: Carrots and radishes are swollen versions of these organs. For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor plants and absorb water.

clues.t: Absorb water and minerals from the soil and anchor the plant in place
Some species grow one thick main one (carrots, dandelions); grasses grow a fibrous mat
Tiny hairs near the tip add huge surface area for soaking up water
Carrots, beets, radishes, and sweet potatoes are swollen ones that store food
Grow down toward gravity (positive gravitropism), the opposite of stems
A protective cap covers the growing tip and is constantly worn away and replaced
Legumes like peas house nitrogen-fixing _Rhizobium_ bacteria in nodules on them
Most plants trade sugar to fungi in partnerships called mycorrhizae, which help them collect water and phosphorus
The radicle, the first part out of a sprouting seed, becomes the first one
Adventitious ones grow from stems or leaves, like corn’s “prop” ones and a banyan’s pillars
Black mangroves grow pneumatophores, “snorkel” ones that poke up out of the mud for air
Behind the tip are zones of cell division, elongation, and maturation
Mosses have no true ones; they cling with thread-like rhizoids
Potatoes are not these organs but underground stems called tubers
Soggy soil can starve them of the oxygen they need for cellular respiration
The Casparian strip, a waxy band of suberin in the endodermis, forces water through cell membranes
New side branches start in the pericycle, just inside the endodermis
Starch-filled statoliths in the cap settle downward to sense gravity
The quiescent center, a cluster of slow-dividing cells at the tip, keeps a reserve of stem cells
Their pressure at night pushes water droplets out of leaf edges (guttation)
Water moves through cell walls (the apoplast) or through linked cytoplasm (the symplast)
Tree-dwelling orchids have aerial ones wrapped in spongy, silvery velamen
Black walnuts release juglone, partly from them, harming nearby tomatoes (allelopathy)
Their tips make much of a plant’s cytokinins, hormones that trigger cell division
Gardeners dip cuttings in auxin powders like IBA to make new ones sprout
Dodder loses its own after latching onto a host and feeds through haustoria
Contractile ones shrink lengthwise to pull lily bulbs deeper into soil
Cut crosswise, eudicots like buttercups show X-shaped xylem; monocots show a ring around a pith

trap.title: Potatoes are stems!
trap.body: Plenty of underground plant parts are not roots. Potatoes are tubers (swollen underground stems), ginger is a rhizome (another underground stem), and onions are bulbs made of fleshy leaves, while carrots, beets, and sweet potatoes really are roots. Mosses don’t have true roots at all; their rhizoids only look like them.
trap.fix: A potato’s “eyes” are buds growing from nodes, a feature of stems. If the clues mention root hairs, a root cap, a Casparian strip, or absorbing water and minerals, answer roots, not stems or rhizomes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Roots (accept root system or taproot; do not accept “stems,” “tubers,” “rhizomes,” or “rhizoids”)

topics.name: Teeth
topics.kicker: Enamel-coated structures for biting and chewing · From incisors to molars
topics.briefing: Teeth are covered in enamel, the hardest substance in the human body, yet enamel has no living cells, so it can’t heal itself the way bone does. Under it lies yellowish dentin, and at the center is a soft pulp full of nerves and blood vessels. Children grow 20 baby teeth, which give way to 32 permanent ones, from sharp incisors in front to flat, grinding molars in back.
topics.answerHtml: Teeth (accept tooth or dentition; prompt on specific kinds such as molars, incisors, or canines; do not accept “enamel” or “bones”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Pierre Fauchard [“foh-SHAR”], called the father of modern dentistry, wrote a 1728 book about caring for these structures, _The Surgeon Dentist_. Beneath their outer layer is a yellowish tissue called dentin, and at their center is a soft pulp filled with nerves and blood vessels.
tossups.r: Their outer covering, enamel, is the hardest substance in the human body. For 10 points, name these structures, including molars and incisors, that are used to chew food.

tossups.p: After the Battle of Bunker Hill, Paul Revere identified the body of his friend Joseph Warren by recognizing a wired-in replacement he had made for one of these structures. Revere, a silversmith, also advertised that he could fit people with artificial ones.
tossups.r: Adults normally have 32 of these structures, while children have 20. For 10 points, name these hard structures in the mouth, such as canines and molars.

tossups.p: Contrary to legend, George Washington’s replacements for these structures were not made of wood; one set was carved partly from hippopotamus ivory. When he became president in 1789, Washington had only one of his own left.
tossups.r: Dentists check these structures for cavities. For 10 points, name these structures covered in enamel, which include incisors, canines, and molars.

tossups.p: Frederick McKay studied a “Colorado brown stain” on these structures in Colorado Springs and noticed that people with the stain had surprisingly few cavities. That stain was traced to fluoride in the water, and in 1945 Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add fluoride to its water supply.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these structures whose outer layer, enamel, is the hardest substance in the human body.

tossups.p: Cells called ameloblasts [“uh-MEL-oh-blasts”] build the outer layer of these structures but are lost once the structures emerge, so that layer can never grow back. Cells called odontoblasts [“oh-DON-toh-blasts”] make these structures’ dentin, which is full of tiny tubes.
tossups.r: These structures sit in sockets in the jaw. For 10 points, name these structures, including molars, whose enamel is the hardest substance in the body.

tossups.p: Biologists summarize these structures with a formula; for adult humans it is 2-1-2-3, a count for each quarter of the mouth. Most mammals are “heterodont,” meaning they have several different kinds of these structures, while many reptiles have only one kind.
tossups.r: Those kinds include incisors, canines, premolars, and molars. For 10 points, name these hard structures used for biting and chewing.

tossups.p: A shark’s skin is covered in dermal denticles [“DEN-tih-kulz”], tiny scales built much like these structures. Sharks constantly replace these structures, which grow in rows and move forward like a conveyor belt as old ones fall out.
tossups.r: Humans get only two sets of these structures: 20 primary ones and 32 permanent ones. For 10 points, name these structures used for chewing.

tossups.p: A beaver’s front examples of these structures are orange because of iron in their enamel, and in all rodents those front incisors never stop growing, so the animals must gnaw to wear them down. Elephant tusks are actually giant incisors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hard structures in the mouths of most mammals, which include canines and molars.

tossups.p: A narwhal’s long tusk, which usually grows out through the upper lip of males, is actually one of these structures, and a walrus’s tusks are extra-long canines. In humans, the last of these structures to come in are the third molars, nicknamed for “wisdom.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these structures, covered in enamel, that people brush and floss to prevent cavities.

tossups.p: The bacterium _Streptococcus mutans_ [“strep-tuh-KOK-us MYOO-tanz”] is a main cause of decay in these structures, because it turns sugar into acid. Sticky plaque on these structures can harden into tartar, which is also called calculus.
tossups.r: Dentists fill cavities in these structures. For 10 points, name these structures, such as incisors and molars, that are covered in enamel.

tossups.p: William Morton’s famous 1846 public demonstration of ether at Massachusetts General Hospital helped launch modern anesthesia. Morton and Horace Wells, who tried laughing gas, were both dentists hoping to spare patients pain when these structures were pulled.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these structures in the mouth, which include canines and premolars and are covered in enamel.

tossups.p: A bone-like layer called cementum covers the root of each of these structures, and the periodontal [“pair-ee-oh-DON-tul”] ligament holds each one in its socket. A root canal treatment removes infected pulp from inside one of these.
tossups.r: The visible part of each of these structures is its crown. For 10 points, name these structures, coated with enamel, that grind and cut food.

tossups.p: The hardest part of these structures is made mostly of a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite [“hy-DROX-ee-AP-uh-tite”], and fluoride helps it resist acid by turning some of it into fluorapatite. Unlike bone, that outer layer contains no living cells, so it cannot repair itself.
tossups.r: That layer is enamel. For 10 points, name these structures, which people use to bite and chew food.

tossups.p: Paleontologists often identify fossil mammals from these structures alone, because their enamel survives so well. _Smilodon_ [“SMY-luh-don”], a big cat of the Ice Age, is famous for two of these structures that grew into long, blade-like canines.
tossups.r: Humans have 32 of these structures as adults. For 10 points, name these structures, including incisors and molars, that are anchored in the jaw.

tossups.p: Dentin forms most of each of these structures, under an outer coating of enamel. Children lose their primary, or “baby,” set of these structures and grow a permanent set, which usually begins with the first molars around age six.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these structures in the mouth, which include incisors for cutting and molars for grinding.

clues.t: Coated in enamel, the hardest substance in the human body
Kinds include incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, and premolars and molars for grinding
Adults have 32 permanent ones; children have 20 primary, or “baby,” ones
Dentists fix cavities, which form when mouth bacteria turn sugar into acid
Each has a visible crown and is anchored in a socket in the jaw
Yellowish dentin, made by odontoblasts, forms most of each one, beneath the enamel
The soft pulp at the center holds nerves and blood vessels; a root canal removes infected pulp
Fluoride helps enamel resist acid; Grand Rapids, Michigan, first added it to city water in 1945
Sticky plaque can harden into tartar, also called calculus
Enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral; it has no living cells, so it can’t repair itself
Cementum coats the root, and the periodontal ligament holds it in its socket
Elephant tusks are giant incisors and walrus tusks are canines; a narwhal’s tusk is one, too
Sharks replace theirs all their lives, in rows that move forward like a conveyor belt
Rodent incisors never stop growing; beavers’ are orange from iron in the enamel
Pierre Fauchard, the “father of modern dentistry,” wrote _The Surgeon Dentist_ (1728)
Paul Revere identified Joseph Warren’s body after Bunker Hill by dental work he had made
George Washington’s dentures weren’t wooden; one set used hippopotamus ivory, and by 1789 he had only one of his own left
Frederick McKay’s study of “Colorado brown stain” in Colorado Springs led to the discovery that fluoride fights cavities
Ameloblasts build enamel and are lost once the structure emerges; odontoblasts build dentin
The adult human dental formula is 2-1-2-3 for each quarter of the mouth
Most mammals are heterodont (several kinds); many reptiles have just one kind
Dentists Horace Wells (laughing gas) and William Morton (ether, 1846) pioneered anesthesia
The bacterium _Streptococcus mutans_ is a main cause of cavities, or decay
Shark skin is covered in dermal denticles, tiny scales built much like them
Paleontologists identify fossil mammals by them; _Smilodon_ had long, blade-like canines
The third molars, nicknamed for “wisdom,” usually come in during the late teens or early twenties

trap.title: Enamel is just one layer
trap.body: Many tossups lead with enamel, “the hardest substance in the human body,” and eager players buzz with “enamel” when the question asks for the whole structure. Others call teeth bones, but they are not: enamel has no living cells and cannot heal. Naming just one kind, like “molars,” is also too narrow when the clues cover every kind.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun: “this substance” or “this tissue” wants enamel or dentin, but “these structures” wants teeth (or tooth). Give a specific kind like molars or canines only if every clue is about that kind.
trap.line: Real answer line: Teeth (accept tooth; prompt on specific kinds like molars or incisors; do not accept “enamel”)

topics.name: Calvin cycle
topics.kicker: Sugar-building stage of photosynthesis · Fixes carbon dioxide in the stroma
topics.briefing: The Calvin cycle is the second half of photosynthesis, where a plant actually builds sugar. In the stroma of each chloroplast, the enzyme RuBisCO grabs carbon dioxide from the air, and the cycle spends ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to turn it into a three-carbon sugar called G3P. Melvin Calvin’s team at Berkeley worked out its steps by tracing radioactive carbon through algae, earning him the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
topics.answerHtml: Calvin cycle (accept Calvin–Benson cycle, Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle, CBB cycle, light-independent reactions, or dark reactions; prompt on carbon fixation; do not accept “photosynthesis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The radioactive tracer used to work out this process, carbon-14, had been discovered at Berkeley in 1940 by Sam Ruben and Martin Kamen. Researchers gave the green alga _Chlorella_ [“kluh-REL-uh”] carbon dioxide made with that tracer and stopped the reactions after a few seconds to see which molecules picked it up first.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle, the second stage of photosynthesis, which turns carbon dioxide into sugar in the stroma.

tossups.p: Algae were bathed in light inside a thin, flat glass flask nicknamed the “lollipop” as scientists traced how this process captures carbon. The resulting molecules were separated by two-dimensional paper chromatography and found by laying X-ray film over the paper, a method called autoradiography.
tossups.r: This process earned its Berkeley namesake the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. For 10 points, name this cycle of photosynthesis that builds sugar from carbon dioxide.

tossups.p: Andrew Benson and James Bassham helped map this process at Berkeley, so their names are sometimes added to its name. This process spends the ATP and NADPH made by the light-capturing reactions in the thylakoid membranes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle that takes place in the stroma of chloroplasts and fixes carbon dioxide into sugar.

tossups.p: When this process’s first enzyme grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, especially on hot, dry days, the cell wastes energy in a process called photorespiration. That enzyme, RuBisCO [“roo-BISS-koh”], is slow, handling only a few molecules each second, so leaves pack in huge amounts of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sugar-building cycle, the second stage of photosynthesis, which takes place in the stroma.

tossups.p: Corn and sugarcane first trap carbon dioxide in a four-carbon acid using PEP carboxylase [“kar-BOK-sih-lays”], then release it in bundle-sheath cells where this process runs, in a pathway named for Marshall Hatch and Roger Slack. That arrangement of cells is called Kranz anatomy, from the German word for “wreath.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle of reactions in the stroma that uses ATP and NADPH to turn carbon dioxide into sugar.

tossups.p: Pineapples and cacti open their pores only at night, storing carbon dioxide as malic acid, and then run this process during the day with their pores closed to save water. That strategy is called crassulacean [“kras-yoo-LAY-shun”] acid metabolism, or CAM.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle, the second stage of photosynthesis, which builds sugar in the stroma of chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Most plants are called “C3” plants because this process’s first stable product, 3-phosphoglycerate [“FOS-foh-GLISS-er-ate”], has three carbon atoms. That product forms when a five-carbon sugar called RuBP takes on carbon dioxide and the resulting six-carbon molecule splits in two.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle, the stage of photosynthesis that uses carbon dioxide to build sugar.

tossups.p: For every six molecules of G3P made by this process, five are rearranged to rebuild three molecules of RuBP, and only one leaves to help build glucose. Making one glucose molecule takes six turns of this process, 18 ATP, and 12 NADPH.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle in the stroma of chloroplasts that fixes carbon dioxide into sugar.

tossups.p: Cyanobacteria speed up this process by packing its key enzyme inside protein shells called carboxysomes [“kar-BOK-sih-sohmz”], which concentrate carbon dioxide. Some bacteria that get energy from chemicals instead of light also use this process to fix carbon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle, the second stage of photosynthesis, which makes sugar in the stroma of chloroplasts.

tossups.p: This process is often divided into three phases: carbon fixation, reduction, and the regeneration of RuBP. In the reduction phase, energy from ATP and electrons from NADPH convert 3-PGA into a three-carbon sugar.
tossups.r: This process uses carbon dioxide that enters leaves through stomata. For 10 points, name this cycle of photosynthesis that takes place in the stroma.

tossups.p: The direct product of this process is glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate [“GLISS-er-AL-duh-hyde three FOS-fate”], a three-carbon sugar often shortened to G3P. That sugar can be turned into sucrose and shipped through the phloem, or stored in the chloroplast as starch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle that uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide.

tossups.p: The enzyme that starts this process, RuBisCO, is often called the most abundant protein on Earth. That enzyme attaches carbon dioxide to a five-carbon sugar called RuBP in a step called carbon fixation.
tossups.r: This process is named for a chemist who won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. For 10 points, name this cycle, the second stage of photosynthesis.

tossups.p: An old nickname for this process wrongly suggests that it happens in darkness, but it mostly runs in daylight, when the light reactions keep making the ATP and NADPH it needs. In the dark, this process soon stops as those supplies run out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle in the chloroplast’s stroma that turns carbon dioxide into sugar.

tossups.p: This process sends ADP and NADP+ [“N-A-D-P-plus”] back to the thylakoid membranes, where the light reactions recharge them. It does not use light directly, but depends on the ATP and NADPH made in those membranes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cycle, the sugar-building stage of photosynthesis, which takes place in the stroma.

tossups.p: Carbon dioxide that enters a leaf through tiny pores called stomata diffuses into chloroplasts, where this process builds it into sugar. This process uses the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second stage of photosynthesis, a cycle named for a Nobel Prize–winning chemist from Berkeley.

Three phases: carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration of RuBP
Its direct product is G3P (glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate), a three-carbon sugar
Fixing carbon dioxide to five-carbon RuBP makes a six-carbon molecule that splits into two 3-PGA
An old nickname wrongly suggests it runs in the dark; it mostly runs in daylight
Mapped by giving _Chlorella_ algae carbon dioxide made with radioactive carbon-14
One glucose takes six turns, 18 ATP, and 12 NADPH
Its sugar becomes sucrose (shipped through phloem) or starch (stored in the chloroplast)
Algae were lit inside a flat glass flask nicknamed the “lollipop”
Its molecules were sorted by two-dimensional paper chromatography and spotted with X-ray film (autoradiography)
Carbon-14 was discovered at Berkeley in 1940 by Sam Ruben and Martin Kamen
When RuBisCO grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, energy is wasted in photorespiration
RuBisCO is slow, handling only a few molecules per second, so leaves pack in huge amounts
C4 species like corn trap carbon dioxide with PEP carboxylase and run it in bundle-sheath cells (Kranz anatomy, the Hatch–Slack pathway)
CAM species like pineapples and cacti store carbon dioxide as malic acid at night and run it by day
Most species are “C3” because its first stable product, 3-PGA, has three carbons
Andrew Benson and James Bassham helped map it at Berkeley, so their names are sometimes added to its name
Of every six G3P it makes, five rebuild three RuBP and only one leaves
Cyanobacteria pack its key enzyme into protein shells called carboxysomes
Some bacteria that get energy from chemicals instead of light also use it to fix carbon
It sends ADP and NADP+ back to the thylakoids to be recharged

trap.title: Part, not the whole
trap.body: This cycle is only the second half of photosynthesis, so players who hear “chloroplast” or “carbon dioxide” often blurt “photosynthesis,” which is too general. Others mix it up with the light reactions, which happen in the thylakoids and split water, or with the Krebs cycle, the cycle in mitochondria that breaks sugar down instead of building it up.
trap.fix: Clues about the stroma, RuBisCO, RuBP, G3P, or spending ATP and NADPH mean the Calvin cycle. Water splitting, oxygen release, or photosystems mean the light reactions; acetyl-CoA or the mitochondrial matrix means the Krebs cycle.
trap.line: Real answer line: Calvin cycle (accept Calvin–Benson cycle or light-independent reactions; accept dark reactions; prompt on carbon fixation; do not accept “photosynthesis”)
